rows.b: A drum-memory machine that became the most popular computer of its decade, used for payroll, grades, and science alike. Programs were loaded from punched cards.
IBM's first commercial scientific computer, renting to aircraft companies and government labs. It used electrostatic storage tubes for memory and magnetic tape for data.
A business machine with an open design that other companies could copy, which created the clone industry. Its slot architecture and DOS software became the world standard.
A line of compatible computers from small business machines to giant mainframes, all running the same programs. It introduced the 8-bit byte as the industry standard.
The whole central processor of a computer on one chip — four bits wide, running at under a megahertz. It was made for a calculator and ended up starting the microprocessor age.
An 8-bit processor on one chip that could address far more memory than the 4004. It powered early hobby machines and terminals.
